milestones.title: Milestone and DAG driven development
milestones.problem: Work in this repository was planned in conversation and in task records that describe one session at a time. There was no executable specification of an outcome, no dependency graph between pieces of work, and no way for a fresh worker to ask the repository what to do next. The tool supervises a task; nothing supervised the plan the task belonged to.
milestones.outcome: Every non-trivial change in this repository belongs to a milestone specification and to one dependency-linked issue execution contract, validated as a DAG, with status derived rather than asserted, and projected to GitHub and to the website from that one canonical model.
milestones.current_state: The canonical model, its engine, its CLI, its projections, its doctrines and its tests exist and are exercised by this milestone's own issues. GitHub carried no issues and no milestones before this work.
milestones.desired_state: A fresh worker with no conversation history runs `majordomus plan next`, receives one issue, executes it inside its declared scope, attaches evidence, and the graph recomputes what is ready without anybody editing a status field.
non_scope: A hosted planning backend or database
A second project-management vocabulary; milestones and issues are the only new nouns
Bidirectional GitHub write-back into the canonical files
Estimation, burndown, velocity or any scheduling model
acceptance_criteria: The canonical model parses, rejects unknown keys, and refuses a duplicate id
A dependency cycle, a self-dependency and an unknown dependency are each rejected with a named finding
READY, BLOCKED, ACTIVE, VERIFY, DONE and CANCELLED are derived from recorded facts and stored nowhere
Execution waves are computed from the graph, and overlapping scope inside one wave is reported
The Mermaid DAG is generated from the same graph the CLI reads
GitHub milestones and issues are created and updated from the canonical model, and drift between them is reported
The website renders the roadmap, every milestone, every issue and the DAG from generated data
Every surface agrees: the CLI, the site data and the GitHub projection report the same issue set and the same READY set
Changing one dependency changes every surface
CI refuses a push whose canonical model is invalid or whose generated artifacts are stale
risks: The engine is shell and awk; a graph large enough to make that slow would need a different implementation. Measured, not assumed.
GitHub is a projection. If a human edits a generated issue body, the next sync reports drift rather than silently overwriting it, which means drift can accumulate unattended.

evidence.result: every case in test/cases passed and none failed, each in a disposable repository
1 passed — the CLI, the JSON output, the Mermaid diagram, the GitHub projection and a freshly generated site-data file agree on every set they can be asked about
1 passed — every canonical mutation the case makes moves every surface
every milestone and issue the model held at this commit existed on korczis/prismatic-majordomus with its state matching the derived status; check exited 0 with no drift

milestones.title: A blocking question survives a handover
milestones.problem: An open question is the mechanism for stopping acceptance when work depends on a person. It is attached to the task that opened it, and the gate only reads questions belonging to the active task. Handing over and starting a new task therefore leaves the question unresolved and no longer blocking anything, so the one thing that was supposed to refuse a completed finish refuses nothing. The gap was found by running the documented end-to-end sequence, not by review, and it is published as a planned claim with no implementation and no test.
milestones.outcome: An unresolved question keeps refusing a completed finish after the work moves to a new task, or the alternative is chosen deliberately and the reason is recorded where the next worker will read it.
milestones.current_state: docs/CLAIMS.yaml carries blocker-survives-handover as planned, with implementation and test both '-'. lib/question.sh matches unresolved lines by the active task id; lib/check.sh reads only those. Nothing detects that a handover has orphaned a blocker.
milestones.desired_state: The behaviour is decided between two named alternatives, implemented, proved by a behavioural case, and the claim moves from planned to guaranteed with its implementation and test filled in.
non_scope: A question that blocks across repositories or worktrees
Assigning a question to a person, or notifying anybody
Any change to the finish contract's other lines
acceptance_criteria: A behavioural case demonstrates the current escape, so the gap is executable rather than asserted
The choice between transferring the question and widening the gate is recorded as a decision with what was rejected and why
The chosen behaviour is implemented and a case fails when it is removed
The claim in docs/CLAIMS.yaml moves to guaranteed with a real implementation path and a real test path
The claim detail page states what the behaviour does not cover
risks: Transferring a question with a handover makes it a property of the work rather than of the task, which is right in the common case and wrong when the handover is to a different piece of work. Widening the gate to every unresolved question blocks tasks that never opened one. The decision has to name the case it is choosing to be wrong in.

evidence.result: the case runs the documented sequence and the mutation section reproduces the escape from a probe that narrows the gate back to the active task, so the gap is executable rather than described
the choice, both rejected alternatives with the case each gets wrong, and the two conditions the choice imposed on the implementation

milestones.title: Cost per accepted outcome, only on measured data
milestones.problem: Cost per token is not a useful unit of work. The unit that matters is what an accepted outcome cost, and that cannot be computed without both telemetry and an acceptance record.
milestones.outcome: The cost of an accepted outcome is computed from measured telemetry and the finish contract that accepted it, and is reported only where both exist.
milestones.current_state: Not started, and not startable: it needs execution telemetry underneath it.
milestones.desired_state: A completed, accepted task can state what it cost, from measurement rather than estimate.
non_scope: Any figure derived from elapsed time or token count as a proxy for progress
acceptance_criteria: Cost is reported only for outcomes that were accepted by the finish contract
An outcome without telemetry reports no cost rather than a modelled one
The denominator is a real acceptance, never a count of sessions
risks: Accepted outcomes are rare enough early on that the number is noisy; it must say so.

milestones.outcome: Execution telemetry is recorded for providers that report it truthfully, and absence is recorded as absence rather than estimated.
milestones.current_state: Not started. docs/ECONOMICS.md states what it would take and deliberately claims nothing.

milestones.title: A supervisory control layer that is real rather than described
milestones.problem: An AI worker in a repository has no durable memory, no declared scope, and no contract that says when its work is finished. Every session starts from nothing and ends by asserting success. The evidence that a rule is enforced is usually a sentence claiming it is.
milestones.outcome: A repository carries one policy, a small set of profiles, durable task state, and a set of commands that refuse work which does not meet a declared contract — with every rule dispatched from a registry that proves it reaches the command claiming to run it.
milestones.current_state: Delivered. The policy, the profiles, the durable records, the command surface, the doctrine registry with wiring reconciliation and the provider projections all exist and are covered by the behavioural suite.
milestones.desired_state: Unchanged: this milestone is the base every later one is measured against.
non_scope: Measuring tokens or cost
Constraining a provider's runtime
acceptance_criteria: One canonical policy projects to every provider and drift is detectable in one command
A task declares scope, and work outside it is reported
A finish contract is evaluated rather than asserted
Every enforced rule is declared in a registry, dispatched from it, and proven to reach its command
Every behaviour has a case in the suite and CI runs it
risks: The floor is bash 3.2 and BSD userland, which bounds what the engine can be asked to do.

evidence.result: the behavioural suite covering the policy, the profiles, the task lifecycle, the doctrine registry and the provider projections passes

milestones.title: Routing recommendations derived from measured cost
milestones.problem: Choosing which capability to send a task to is currently a judgement nobody can check. A recommendation not derived from measured outcomes is an opinion with a command around it.
milestones.outcome: The profile a task should run under is recommended from measured cost per accepted outcome, and the recommendation names the data it came from.
milestones.current_state: Not started, and gated on cost per accepted outcome existing at all.
milestones.desired_state: A worker can ask which profile a class of task should use and get an answer traceable to measurements.
non_scope: Automatic routing without a person's decision
acceptance_criteria: Every recommendation names the measurements it was derived from
Insufficient data produces no recommendation rather than a weak one
The recommendation is advisory and never silently changes a profile
risks: A recommendation that is followed becomes a cause of the data that justifies it.

milestones.title: Profiles become runtime constraints rather than advice
milestones.problem: A profile declares an effort and a verbosity, and then nothing enforces them. The worker reads the projection and is trusted to behave. An axis that only ever appears in generated prose is a preference, not a control.
milestones.outcome: A profile's axes become opt-in runtime clamps a provider actually applies — read size, output condensation, subagent budget — with the limit derived from the profile rather than configured twice.
milestones.current_state: Not started. The profiles exist and project correctly; nothing derives a runtime limit from them.
milestones.desired_state: Starting a task under a profile constrains what the worker may do, and the constraint is visible in the same place the profile is.
non_scope: Provider-specific behaviour that cannot be verified from this repository
acceptance_criteria: At least one runtime limit is derived from the profile and applied, not merely printed
The limit is opt-in and a repository that does not want it is unaffected
A behavioural case proves the limit changes what happens, not only what is reported
risks: Only providers that expose a real knob can be clamped honestly; the rest would be theatre.

milestones.title: Shared policy across repositories and workers
milestones.problem: Policy is per repository. An organisation running many repositories has no way to state a rule once, and no way to see where it is not being followed.
milestones.outcome: A policy can be shared across repositories and workers, with local override remaining explicit and drift from the shared source detectable in one command.
milestones.current_state: Not started. Everything the tool does today is scoped to a single checkout.
milestones.desired_state: One policy statement governs many repositories, and every deviation from it is visible rather than assumed.
non_scope: A hosted service, a registry, or any component that must be running for the tool to work
acceptance_criteria: A shared policy can be consumed by more than one repository without copying it
A local override is explicit and survives an update of the shared source
Drift between the shared policy and a repository's effective policy is reported by one command
risks: Shared policy is where a local tool becomes a distributed one; the offline guarantee has to survive it.

issues.title: Audit what actually plans work in this repository
non_scope: Any change to behaviour
issues.objective: Establish an evidence-backed map of how work is currently planned, tracked and remembered here, so that the model that replaces it is built against reality rather than against the README.
issues.why: Every later issue depends on knowing what already exists. The repository already has a canonical-to-derived architecture for claims, doctrines and the website; a planning model that ignored it would be a second architecture.
issues.current_state: Planning lived in task records, handovers, checkpoints and decisions. GitHub had no milestones and no issues. There was no dependency relation between pieces of work anywhere.
issues.desired_state: The current-state map exists, backed by commands anyone can rerun, and the schema work that follows cites it.
acceptance_criteria: The GitHub milestone and issue inventory is measured, not assumed
The existing canonical-to-derived pipeline is identified so the new model reuses it
The portability constraints that bound the implementation are named

evidence.command: gh issue list --state all --limit 50; gh api repos/korczis/prismatic-majordomus/milestones
evidence.result: both empty: the repository had no GitHub issues and no milestones before this milestone

issues.risk: Low. Read-only.

issues.title: Define the canonical milestone and issue schema
non_scope: JSON Schema; this repository validates with allowlists and its own YAML subset
A separate evidence directory; evidence lives inside the record it proves
issues.objective: Define the smallest repository-native representation of a milestone outcome specification and an issue execution contract, and enforce it the way every other configuration file here is enforced: a key nobody reads is an error.
issues.why: Every surface downstream reads these files. A field that is written and never read, or read and never written, becomes a lie that the website eventually publishes.
issues.current_state: Policy, profiles and prompts each have an allowlist under share/allow. Milestones and issues had none because they did not exist.
issues.desired_state: share/allow/project.txt, share/allow/milestone.txt and share/allow/issue.txt exist and every key in a canonical file matches one of them.
acceptance_criteria: An unknown key in a milestone or issue file is a reported failure
No status field exists in either schema
Evidence is part of the record whose completion it gates

evidence.result: 1 passed, 0 failed

issues.risk: A schema too small forces a later migration; a schema too large invites fields nobody reads.

issues.title: Implement the model loader and the status derivation engine
non_scope: Any status field a human can set directly
issues.objective: Load every canonical file into one normalised model and derive issue and milestone status from recorded facts, in exactly one implementation that every surface calls.
issues.why: Four surfaces need to know what is READY. Four implementations of READY is four answers. One engine is the whole architecture.
issues.current_state: Nothing read the canonical files.
issues.desired_state: lib/project.sh loads the files, lib/project.awk derives the model, and the CLI, the site generator and the GitHub adapter all read that model.
acceptance_criteria: Issue status is derived from started_at, verified_at, completed_at, cancelled, evidence coverage and dependency state
Milestone status is derived from its issues and its own evidence
The active milestone is derived from order and status, not declared
A completed issue whose required evidence is missing derives VERIFY, not DONE

evidence.result: 1 passed, 0 failed

issues.risk: bash 3.2 has no associative arrays; the graph work is done in awk, which does.

issues.title: Implement DAG validation and execution waves
non_scope: Estimation or critical-path scheduling
issues.objective: Validate the dependency graph and derive topological execution waves, refusing every malformed graph with a named finding rather than a guess.
issues.why: A dependency list without validation is a suggestion. A cycle that nobody detects becomes a set of issues that can never be ready and nobody can explain why.
issues.current_state: No graph existed.
issues.desired_state: Unknown, self and duplicate dependencies, duplicate ids and cycles are each rejected by name, and waves are computed by Kahn layering.
acceptance_criteria: A cycle is detected and the issues inside it are named
A self-dependency and an unknown dependency are each a distinct finding
Waves place an issue one layer past its deepest dependency
Two issues sharing a wave and a scope path are reported as serialised

issues.desired_state: One command answers what an accepted outcome cost, in text and as JSON, and where it cannot answer, it names whether acceptance or measurement was missing.
acceptance_criteria: A figure is reported only where a measured record and an accepted outcome both exist
Where no figure is reported, the output names which half was missing
JSON and text agree on the set of outcomes and the figures reported
issues.risk: The first number this command prints will be quoted somewhere; its units and its denominator have to be in the output itself, not only in the documentation.

issues.title: Make a thin denominator say so rather than average it away
non_scope: A confidence interval or any statistical model beyond stating the denominator
issues.objective: Make every reported figure carry the number of accepted outcomes it rests on, refuse to present a single observation as an average, and prove both with cases.
issues.why: Early on there will be very few accepted outcomes, and a mean over one of them looks exactly like a mean over many. The report has to make the difference impossible to miss.
issues.current_state: The command reports figures from whatever measured, accepted outcomes exist, however few.
issues.desired_state: Each figure states its denominator, and below the threshold the output presents observations rather than a summary statistic.
acceptance_criteria: Every reported figure carries the count of accepted outcomes behind it
Below the declared threshold the output presents observations and no average
The threshold is declared as data, not written into the code path
Cases cover the thin case and the sufficient case
issues.risk: Any threshold is arbitrary; declaring it as data and printing it beside the figure is what keeps it honest rather than hidden.

issues.title: Publish the cost-per-outcome claim with its unit defined beside it
non_scope: Any comparison against another tool or another team
issues.objective: Move the cost-per-outcome claim to guaranteed, define the unit and the denominator where a reader meets the figure, and state what the number cannot be used to compare.
issues.why: Cost per accepted outcome is the one figure this project argues is the right unit. Publishing it without saying what it excludes would repeat the mistake the economics document was written to avoid.
issues.current_state: The claim is planned. The economics document argues for the unit and reports nothing.
issues.desired_state: The claim is guaranteed, the unit and denominator are defined next to the reported figure, and the limits of comparison are stated.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The unit and denominator are defined where the figure is presented
The document states what the figure cannot be used to compare
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: A published cost figure is the most quotable thing this repository will produce and the most easily stripped of its qualifiers.

issues.title: Group comparable work from what the records already carry
non_scope: A hand-written taxonomy of task types
Any new noun; the grouping is a derivation, not a record
issues.objective: Derive the grouping that makes two pieces of work comparable from facts the records already hold, so that a recommendation compares like with like without anybody inventing a taxonomy of task types.
issues.why: A recommendation is only meaningful within a class of comparable work, and the obvious way to get one is to invent categories. Invented categories are a new vocabulary nobody validates, which this repository refuses on principle and would regret in practice.
issues.current_state: Records carry a profile, a declared scope, a verification result and an outcome. Nothing groups them, and nothing says what makes two tasks comparable.
issues.desired_state: A derivation produces groups from recorded facts alone, states what it grouped on, and refuses to group where the facts are too thin to support it.
acceptance_criteria: Grouping uses only fields already recorded, and names them in its output
No new record type or vocabulary is introduced
Work that cannot be grouped is reported as ungrouped rather than forced into a group
issues.risk: A grouping that is too coarse makes every recommendation the same one; too fine and no group ever reaches a usable denominator. Whichever is chosen has to be visible in the output.

issues.title: Recommend a profile from measured cost, naming the measurements
non_scope: Invoking a model, or choosing a provider on a worker's behalf
issues.objective: Add the command that recommends a profile for a class of work from measured cost per accepted outcome, and prints the measurements the recommendation was derived from alongside it.
issues.why: A recommendation whose basis is not printed is an opinion with a command around it. Naming the measurements is what makes it checkable, and being checkable is the only thing that separates this from advice.
issues.current_state: Cost per accepted outcome is reported per outcome. Nothing recommends anything.
issues.desired_state: Asking which profile a class of work should use returns a profile, the measurements behind it, and the group they came from.
acceptance_criteria: Every recommendation lists the accepted outcomes and figures it was derived from
The recommendation names the group and how the group was derived
The command reads records and computes nothing that the cost layer already computes
issues.risk: Following a recommendation produces the data that justifies it; the output has to record that the measurements postdate earlier recommendations.

issues.title: Return no recommendation where the data is too thin, and say why
non_scope: A weaker recommendation with a caveat attached
issues.objective: Make insufficient data produce no recommendation rather than a weak one, with the threshold declared as data and the reason printed, proved by cases on both sides of it.
issues.why: The failure mode of every routing feature is a confident answer from three data points. Refusing to answer is the behaviour that has to be tested, because it is the one that will be pressured away.
issues.current_state: The command recommends from whatever measurements exist.
issues.desired_state: Below the threshold the command returns no recommendation and names what it would take to have one; above it, the recommendation carries its denominator.
acceptance_criteria: The threshold is declared as data and printed with every answer and every refusal
Below it, no profile is named at all
Cases cover both sides of the threshold
issues.risk: A threshold nobody can reach makes the whole command dead code; if the case shows the bar is unreachable in practice, that is a finding about the milestone, not a reason to lower it quietly.

issues.title: Prove the recommendation is advisory and publish it as such
non_scope: Any automatic application of a recommendation, behind a flag or otherwise
issues.objective: Prove with a case that a recommendation never changes the profile a task runs under, and publish the routing claim stating that Majordomus recommends and does not route.
issues.why: The distance between recommending a profile and selecting one is one convenience commit wide. A case is the only thing that keeps it, and the claim is where a reader is told which side of the line the tool is on.
issues.current_state: The command answers with a profile and a basis. Nothing proves it cannot act on its own answer.
issues.desired_state: A case starts a task after a recommendation and shows the profile is whatever the worker asked for, and the claim says recommendations only.
acceptance_criteria: A case shows a task starting under a profile different from the recommended one, unimpeded
The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist and says recommendations only
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: A tool that recommends is one flag away from a tool that decides; the case is the record of the decision not to add the flag.

issues.title: Let a policy name a shared source it does not copy
non_scope: Fetching a policy over a network, from a registry, or from any service
A hosted component that must be running for the tool to work
issues.objective: Let a repository's policy name a shared policy source and resolve it offline from the filesystem, so that one statement of a rule can govern more than one repository without being pasted into each.
issues.why: Copying is what makes organisational policy drift: every repository holds a fork of the rule and nobody can see which forks moved. A named source is the smallest change that makes drift detectable at all.
issues.current_state: Policy is per repository and entirely local. Nothing refers to anything outside the checkout.
issues.desired_state: A policy names a shared source, the tool resolves it without a network call, and every command that reads policy reads the resolved result.
acceptance_criteria: A shared source is resolved from the filesystem with no network access
Every policy reader sees the resolved policy, and no reader bypasses resolution
An unresolvable source is a named finding that stops the command, never a silent fallback to local
A repository that names no shared source behaves exactly as it does today
issues.risk: This is where a local-first tool grows a dependency outside its checkout; keeping resolution to the filesystem is what preserves the offline guarantee.

issues.title: Make a local override explicit and prove it survives an update of the shared source
non_scope: Overriding a rule the shared policy declares non-overridable, if such a class is introduced later
issues.objective: Define how a repository overrides part of a shared policy, require the override to be declared rather than inferred from a value differing, and prove with a case that updating the shared source leaves the override standing.
issues.why: An override that looks like an ordinary key is indistinguishable from a stale copy. Declaring it is what lets the drift report tell a deliberate exception from an accident.
issues.current_state: A shared source can be named and resolved. Anything a repository writes locally either wins or loses by a rule nobody has written down.
issues.desired_state: Overrides are declared, the merge order is documented and tested, and a shared source that changes underneath a repository does not silently take an override away.
acceptance_criteria: An override is a declaration, and a local value that differs without one is a finding
The merge order is documented and covered by a case
A case updates the shared source and shows the override still applies
issues.risk: Merge semantics are where shared configuration usually becomes unexplainable; the documented order and its case are the whole defence.

issues.title: Report drift from the shared policy in one command
non_scope: Changing anybody's policy; the command reports and never writes
issues.objective: Report, in one command, every way a repository's effective policy differs from the shared source it names, separating declared overrides from undeclared divergence.
issues.why: The point of naming a shared source is being able to see where it is not being followed. Without one command that answers that, shared policy is just a longer path to the same drift.
issues.current_state: A shared source is resolved and overrides are declared. Nothing summarises the difference.
issues.desired_state: One command lists each difference, says whether it is a declared override or undeclared divergence, and names the reproduce command for each.
acceptance_criteria: Every difference is listed with the key, both values, and whether it is declared
Undeclared divergence exits non-zero and declared overrides do not
Every finding carries a reproduce command
The command writes nothing
issues.risk: A drift report that is noisy is a drift report nobody runs; declared overrides have to be quiet by default.

issues.title: Prove the offline guarantee survives sharing
non_scope: Any offline cache of a remote source, which would be a fetch with extra steps
issues.objective: Prove with cases and a doctrine that no path introduced by shared policy reaches a network, and that an unavailable shared source degrades to a named refusal rather than a fetch or a silent local fallback.
issues.why: Every guarantee this tool makes rests on it being local and offline. Sharing policy across repositories is the exact feature that historically converts a local tool into a client of something, and it has to be refused structurally rather than by intention.
issues.current_state: Resolution, override and drift reporting all exist and are documented as filesystem-only. Nothing enforces that they stay so.
issues.desired_state: A doctrine refuses a network call in the policy resolution path, cases cover an unavailable source, and the refusal names the doctrine.
acceptance_criteria: A doctrine declares the rule, its validator exists, and doctor proves it reaches the command that runs it
A case shows an unavailable shared source producing a named refusal, with nothing fetched and no fallback
CI runs the case
issues.risk: The pressure to add a remote source arrives with the first user who has repositories on two machines; the doctrine is what makes that a decision rather than a patch.

issues.title: Publish the shared-policy claim and what sharing still cannot do
non_scope: Any claim about repositories that have not adopted the shared source
issues.objective: Move the shared-policy claim to guaranteed, cite the implementation and the cases, and state plainly what a shared policy does not provide: no service, no registry, no cross-machine visibility, and no enforcement of a repository that never adopts it.
issues.why: Shared policy is the version most easily read as an organisational control plane. The claim has to name the boundary in the same place it names the capability, or the boundary will be assumed away.
issues.current_state: The claim is planned, and the design document places multi-repository policy outside the local-first scope with a note that it returns here.
issues.desired_state: The claim is guaranteed for what is implemented, the limitations page names what it is not, and the design document's deferral is reconciled with what now exists.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The limitations page names what shared policy does not do
The design document no longer defers what has shipped, and still refuses what has not
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: This claim is the one a reader will most want to be wider than it is.
